synopsis: These standards provide general engineering discipline rather than collision- or brake-specific requirements: they structure an evidence plan linking claims to evidence, methods, acceptance criteria, owners and gates, but do not determine what to test [f15344, f15345, f15357]. ISO/IEC/IEEE 15288:2023, INCOSE’s 2023 handbook, NASA’s handbook and IEEE 1012 underpin verification and validation planning; ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119-3:2021 and Part 4:2021 supply test-documentation structures and test-design techniques without collision-avoidance content [f9537, f15347, f7112, f7113, f7114]. ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010:2022 supports architecture views tailored to their audience, with a recommended 2–3-page capability and architecture section and a toolchain description distinguishing real, modeled, emulated and substituted elements [f9886, f10160, f15352]. ISO/IEC/IEEE 15026-2:2022 structures assurance arguments from claims through evidence, addressing the program’s ultimate question of whether a safety board can trust a virtual result enough to support a safety decision [f15353, f15356]. ISO 31000:2018 and IEC 31010:2019 underpin risk-register practice, but the booklet identifies thin outcome evidence for risk registers [f15354, f15355].
